chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about eating the locust, so he (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem with eating it.' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'It is a spawn/offspring of the fish in the sea.' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'Ali (peace be upon him) said: The fish and the locusts, when they come out from the water, are pure (sacrificed), and the land is a trap for the locusts, and for the fish it may also be (a trap).'

key_terms.حُوتٍ: Fish/Whale (used here for large sea creatures)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating locusts in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) affirms the permissibility of locusts by likening them to fish, noting that while fish require water to be considered slaughtered, locusts are deemed pure (dhaki) upon leaving the water and landing on land, which serves as their natural trap. This narration highlights the unique jurisprudential status of locusts in Shia fiqh, distinguishing them from other insects by granting them the same ease of consumption as fish without the need for ritual slaughter. The reference to Imam Ali (peace be upon him) underscores the continuity of this ruling from the early Imams, reinforcing its authenticity and practical application for believers.
